question: What is the main focus of embryology?

options.A: The analysis of genetic mutations during adult life
options.B: The microscopic examination of human bone tissue
options.C: The study of prenatal development from fertilization to birth
options.D: The physical changes that occur during normal aging

explanation: Embryology simply looks at how a new baby grows and develops inside the womb, right from the very first cell union up until birth. You've got this! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is a basic knowledge of embryology important for nurses and midwives?

options.A: It helps anticipate birth defects and guide expectant mothers
options.B: It is required to calculate the exact adult height of a child
options.C: It prevents all types of infectious diseases in newborns
options.D: It allows nurses to perform surgical deliveries independently

explanation: Knowing normal pregnancy milestones helps you spot issues early and give wonderful, reassuring health education to pregnant mums in the clinic! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h1)

question: What do we call the process of forming mature sperm cells in the male testes?
explanation: Spermatogenesis is just the medical term for how sperm cells are made in the testes. Think: 'spermato-' for sperm and '-genesis' for creation! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is a major difference between spermatogenesis and oogenesis?

options.A: Oogenesis occurs continuously, while spermatogenesis happens only once a month
options.B: Spermatogenesis results in diploid cells, while oogenesis results in haploid cells
options.C: Spermatogenesis creates polar bodies, while oogenesis creates active swimming cells
options.D: Oogenesis produces one large ovum, while spermatogenesis produces four small sperm

explanation: Egg production saves all its nutrients to make one strong, large ovum, while sperm production creates four nimble swimmers. Nature is fascinating! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h2)

question: Where in the female reproductive tract does fertilization most commonly take place?
explanation: The ampulla of the fallopian tube is the usual meeting place for the sperm and the egg. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h3)

question: Why is the cortical reaction important right when fertilization happens?

options.A: It prevents more than one sperm from entering the egg
options.B: It helps the fertilized egg travel down the fallopian tube
options.C: It provides extra energy for the newly formed zygote
options.D: It speeds up the process of genetic material fusion

explanation: Once the first lucky sperm gets inside, the egg quickly changes its outer coat to lock out all other sperm. It's like a VIP bouncer keeping things orderly! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is the name of the fluid-filled structure that implants into the lining of the womb?
explanation: The blastocyst is the gorgeous little ball of cells ready to nestle comfortably into the uterine lining. You're doing brilliantly with these terms! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h4)

question: During early cleavage (cell division), what happens to the overall size of the cell mass?

options.A: It shrinks drastically because cells lose their water content
options.B: It grows rapidly in size as each cell feeds and expands
options.C: It flattens out into a sheet of tissue inside the tube
options.D: It stays roughly the same while cell numbers increase

explanation: Even though the cells are multiplying rapidly, they all stay snug inside the original protective shell (zona pellucida) so the total size remains similar at first. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which hormone is secreted by the early trophoblast cells to signal pregnancy?
explanation: hCG is the primary hormone detected in pregnancy tests, produced by the cells that attach to the uterine wall. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h5)

question: A patient asks why her body doesn't reject the developing pregnancy as a foreign object. What is the best way to explain this?

options.A: The baby carries the exact same blood type as the mother always
options.B: The placenta completely blocks all maternal blood cells from forming
options.C: The mother's immune system shuts down completely during pregnancy
options.D: The outer trophoblast layer actively modifies local immune responses

explanation: The placenta and outer cells are clever—they whisper to the immune system to stay calm so the baby can grow safely. Clinical communication made simple! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which embryonic germ layer gives rise to the nervous system and skin?
explanation: Think 'ecto' for outer—the outer layer builds things that face the outside world, like your skin and your brain/nerves! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h6)

question: Why is gastrulation such a huge milestone in early human development?

options.A: It marks the exact moment the heart starts its very first visible beat
options.B: It immediately connects the baby's blood supply to the maternal heart
options.C: It causes the embryo to double in size within a single day
options.D: It establishes the three distinct tissue layers that build all body organs

explanation: Gastrulation is like laying down the foundational blueprint (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) needed to construct every single organ in the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h6)

question: The neural tube, which forms the brain and spinal cord, develops from which germ layer?
explanation: Since the nervous system links closely with the skin and outer structures, it comes right from the ectoderm layer. Excellent recall! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h7)

question: Why is organogenesis (organ formation) a time of high vulnerability for the embryo?

options.A: Major body organs are rapidly forming and can be easily disrupted by harmful agents
options.B: The mother's immune system attacks the organs because they are immature
options.C: The placenta has not yet formed to provide any nutrients to the cells
options.D: Cells stop dividing entirely during this phase to rest and repair themselves

explanation: Because body structures are actively being sculpted during this window, harmful substances (teratogens) can easily cause permanent damage. This is why early prenatal care advice is so crucial! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h7)

question: Which vitamin supplement is widely recommended before and during early pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects?
explanation: Folic acid is a true champion for preventing neural tube defects like spina bifida. Every midwife and nurse loves promoting this in antenatal health talks! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h8)

question: Which of these conditions is NOT a result of early embryonic developmental errors?

options.A: Spina bifida caused by incomplete neural tube closure
options.B: Spontaneous miscarriage due to severe chromosomal abnormalities
options.C: Type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed in late adulthood
options.D: Congenital heart defects from abnormal tissue septation

explanation: Type 2 diabetes is a metabolic condition related to later lifestyle and genetics, unlike birth defects caused during early pregnancy development. You're crushing it! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T6#GNS111_U1_T6_h8)
